citeAs: Clark, Christopher, Kenton Lee, Ming-Wei Chang, Tom Kwiatkowski, Michael Collins, and Kristina Toutanova. (2019). BoolQ: Exploring the Surprising Difficulty of Natural Yes/No Questions. arXiv.
creator: Christopher Clark, Kenton Lee, Ming-Wei Chang, Tom Kwiatkowski, Michael Collins, Kristina Toutanova (Google AI Language)
description: BoolQ is a reading comprehension dataset of naturally occurring yes/no questions. Each example consists of a question, a Wikipedia passage, the article title, and a yes/no answer, with questions gathered from anonymized Google search queries and paired with passages selected by human annotators.
name: BoolQ
rai:annotationsPerItem: 1 for the main train/dev/test sets; 110 randomly chosen examples were additionally labeled by three of the authors for annotation quality assessment.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: To assess annotation quality, three of the authors labeled 110 randomly chosen examples and resolved disagreements by mutual agreement to create gold-standard labels. On these 110 examples, the answer annotations reached 90% accuracy compared to the gold-standard labels; six disagreements were ambiguous or debatable cases and five were annotator errors.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators labeled question/article pairs in a three-step process: they first judged whether the question was good, meaning comprehensible, unambiguous, and requesting factual information, before seeing the Wikipedia page; for good questions they then found a passage in the document containing enough information to answer the question or marked it not answerable; finally they labeled the answer as yes or no.
rai:dataBiases: The paper notes that yes answers are slightly more common, with 62.31% in the train set. It also describes design choices intended to reduce bias and artificiality, such as using naturally occurring questions authored by people who were not prompted to write yes/no questions and who did not know the answer, and pairing questions with selected passages to reduce ambiguity and conflicting answers within full documents.
rai:dataCollection: Questions were gathered from anonymized, aggregated Google search queries. Likely yes/no questions were heuristically identified, and only questions with a Wikipedia page among the first five search results were kept. Human annotators then judged question quality, selected an answer-containing passage from the Wikipedia article or marked it not answerable, and labeled the answer yes or no. The dataset combines 13k questions gathered through this pipeline with an additional 3k yes/no questions from the Natural Questions training set, for a total of 16k questions.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: The source data are anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine and corresponding Wikipedia articles. The final examples include a question, a paragraph from a Wikipedia article, the article title, and a yes/no answer.
rai:dataCollectionType: User-generated content data, Software Collection, Document analysis, Manual Human Curator
rai:dataLimitations: The paper reports that yes answers are slightly more common than no answers. It also notes that the dataset uses selected passages rather than full documents, which keeps inputs small enough for existing entailment models but makes it not document-level. The authors state that future work could build a document-level version to increase difficulty and correspondence to an end-user application. They also note that some annotation disagreements were ambiguous or debatable cases.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The collection pipeline included heuristic filtering to identify likely yes/no questions using a manually constructed set of indicator first words and a minimum length requirement. The authors also filtered to cases where a Wikipedia page appeared in the top five search results, used only questions marked as having a yes/no answer, paired each question with the selected passage instead of the full document to reduce ambiguity, and combined 13k newly gathered questions with 3k yes/no questions from the Natural Questions training set. They split the data into 9.4k train, 3.2k dev, and 3.2k test, ensuring questions from Natural Questions were always in the train set.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended for evaluating and training reading comprehension and natural language understanding systems on natural yes/no question answering, especially questions requiring inference and entailment-like reasoning. The paper also presents it as being directly related to the practical end-task of answering user yes/no questions.
